title: 3D Printing 3
tags: openscad, claude-code, parametric-design, reverse-engineering, image-fitting, rear-light
content:
The bike already had a front light, so I added a rear light while I had the bike in pieces and the soldering iron out. This is a side project, and it is not directly related to the [ATtiny85 speed limiter](/posts/attiny2/) that I was building at the same time. The light needed a 3D printed copy of one half of the black block that sits on its back. The block is 105 mm long, 28 mm wide, and 8 mm deep. It carries two studs, two screws, and the cable. I had a first parametric model in OpenSCAD and a first print, and neither was quite right. This post is about the long run of small corrections that got the copy to fit the original and the part that mates with it. ![](assets/images/3dprinting3/finished-rear-light.jpg) *The finished printed block half on the back of the rear light, with the two studs and the cable* ![](assets/images/3dprinting3/finished-back-plate.jpg) *The other side of the finished part, with the two countersunk screws and the studs* I worked with Claude Code in VS Code. Claude Code edited the model, exported the STL, and rendered it so I could check each change before I printed it. The model and the STL are in the [bikespeed repository](https://github.com/Haddley/bikespeed/tree/main/rearlight). ```mermaid flowchart LR A["I describe a problem
or photograph the print"] --> B["Claude Code edits
fuse_block.scad"] B --> C["Claude Code exports the STL
and renders it"] C --> D["I print it and compare
it with the original"] D --> A ``` *Every change went round this loop* ## The part The part is an open tray. Its outer wall is the rim. Inside the rim is a gutter, then a low inner wall. Two large bosses carry the studs, each with a hex pocket for the nut. Two smaller pillars carry the screws. A hole in the middle takes the cable, and four deep slots sit in the gutters. The outside face is flat. ![](assets/images/3dprinting3/openscad-tray.png) *The tray side in OpenSCAD: the rim, the gutter, the inner wall, the two stud bosses with hex pockets, the two screw pillars, the cable hole, and the slots* ![](assets/images/3dprinting3/openscad-outside.png) *The flat outside face, with the countersunk screw holes and the stud and cable holes* ## Beat 1 — Small fixes after the first print The first print was close, but a few features were wrong. I described each one to Claude Code in plain words. ```PROMPT rearlight fuse_block issues... bold head recess is too big please make smaller ``` Claude Code found the hex pocket around each stud hole and reduced it from 9 mm to 8 mm across the flats. ```PROMPT screw hole on the "ouside" need to be wider (countersunk) can be a little more narrow in the "inside" ``` Claude Code added a 90° countersink on the outside face and narrowed the shaft from 4.5 mm to 4.0 mm. ```PROMPT the deep slots in the gutters above and below the screw holes all need to be shifted towards the center of the piece by 2mm (ish). move left deep slots right 2mm and move right deepslots left by 2mm ``` Claude Code moved the four slots 2 mm toward the centre. It made the shift a parameter, `clip_shift`, so I could change it later. :::watch-it The STL on disk is not the model After the countersink change, I looked at the part and wrote that I could not see any countersink on the outside. Claude Code had edited the `.scad` file, but OpenSCAD was not installed on this Mac, so it could not export a new STL. The STL still held the old shape. Homebrew had disabled the normal OpenSCAD cask, so Claude Code installed the snapshot build instead. From then on it re-exported the STL after every change and rendered the part, so I could check the result before I printed. ::: I later made the countersink deeper. My first reading of that request was wrong: Claude Code made it 4 mm deep and 12 mm wide, and I wanted it deeper but not wider. The final version keeps the 8 mm opening. A 2 mm cone narrows to the 4 mm shaft, and a straight 8 mm bore sits above it, so a screw head sits 2 mm below the outside face. ## Beat 2 — Tracing the original To compare the print with the original, I traced around both parts on a sheet of paper. I used the two screw holes as a common reference point and marked them as dots. I drew the new part in red and the original in pencil. ```PROMPT the original and our copy fuse_block parts are a little different. I have traced around the two using the screw holes as a common point of reference. what do you suggest? ``` ![](assets/images/3dprinting3/first-print-and-trace.jpg) *The first printed copy at the top, the trace in the middle, and the original at the bottom* ![](assets/images/3dprinting3/trace-closeup-first.jpg) *A closeup of the left end: the pencil line of the original and the red line of the copy* Claude Code read the photo and told me that our outline looked larger. I could see that it was wrong, because I had measured the two parts by hand. ```PROMPT our outline is not as large vertically as we look at it. from the external most measurement our part is 2mm smaller vertically. Can you see that? ``` The original was 2 mm taller, not shorter. Claude Code changed the height from 26 mm to 28 mm and assumed that the extra 2 mm split evenly above and below the screw holes. That was also wrong. The extra height was all on one side of the holes, so the hole line moved off the centre. :::brain-power Can a photo be a ruler? A photo of a trace has no scale on it, and it is taken at a slight angle. Is there any way to turn it into millimetres without putting a ruler in the picture? Think about what the photo does contain before you read on. ::: ## Beat 3 — Letting the photo be the measuring tape I had one thing in the picture that I already knew exactly: the red line is the outline of our own model. Claude Code used it to work out the scale and the position of the photo, and then read the pencil line of the original in millimetres. :::under-the-hood How the measurement works 1.
